passage: Minutes of the Harlow Green parks committee, taken verbatim by request. Chair Voss: Item three, the playground surface. Quotes are in from two firms. Denner: Read the numbers, please. Chair Voss: Fenmore Surfacing bids 48,000 dollars for poured rubber, twelve week lead time. Ostrand Play bids 39,500 for tile, available in four weeks. Piotrowski: The tile at Weld Park lifted at the corners within two years. We patched it twice last summer. Denner: And the poured surface at the school has been down nine years without a complaint. Chair Voss: The budget line holds 42,000. Piotrowski: Then we are choosing between a surface we can afford that fails and one we trust that we cannot afford. Denner: Ask Fenmore to phase it. Do the toddler area this year, the rest in spring. Chair Voss: Their quote splits at 21,000 now and 29,000 later, which loses us the combined discount. Ostrand will not phase. Piotrowski: I move we take Fenmore phased, toddler area first. Denner: Second. Chair Voss: Discussion? Hearing none. In favor, four. Opposed, none. Abstaining, one, Mr. Aldous, who notes his brother drives for Fenmore. Carried. Item four, the drinking fountain.
question: How much did Ostrand Play bid for the tile surface?

passage: Transcript, staff meeting, Corben Valley Veterinary Clinic, Monday 8 a.m. Dr. Ferro: Quick one today. First, the X-ray machine. The part is on back order until the 19th, so all imaging goes to the Millbrook clinic until then. Book their 2 p.m. slot, they are holding it for us. Reception, that means warning clients about the extra drive. Tansy: Already in the booking notes. Dr. Ferro: Second, the kennel cough cases. We are at eleven confirmed this month, which for us is an outbreak. Until further notice, coughing dogs come through the side door, straight to room 3, and room 3 gets the full wipe down after every one of them. No exceptions, even if it books us solid. Dr. Ilves: The Braithwaite spaniel from Saturday makes it twelve, the lab called this morning. Dr. Ferro: Twelve, then. Third thing: Saturday emergency cover. I have done six of the last eight weekends. Dr. Ilves: Not by my count. Dr. Ferro: By the rota on the wall, which I will be photographing at lunch. We are hiring a locum for two Saturdays a month starting next month, approved by the partners on Thursday. Tansy: Does the locum get a key? Dr. Ferro: The locum gets Marta's old key, which brings me to the last item: Marta, after nineteen years, has given notice for June. We will do this properly closer to the date, but I wanted it said plainly before the rumor got there first. Back to work.
question: To which room do coughing dogs go?

passage: Transcript of the Weybrook library board, budget session, item two. Chair Ambrose: The heating estimate came in at 9,800 dollars, which is 3,300 over what we set aside. Options, Gwen. Treasurer Holm: Three. Defer the local history room shelving, which frees 2,100. Cancel the author series, 1,400. Or draw down the reserve, which stands at 8,000 and which we drained to 2,000 after the flood in 2019 and swore never again. Marchetti: The author series sells memberships. We gained 41 members after last spring's series, I checked the ledger. Chair Ambrose: And the shelving? Kwon: The shelving has been deferred twice already. The boxes from the Pruett estate have sat unopened for fourteen months, and Mrs. Pruett's son asks me about them at church, every week, without fail. Treasurer Holm: Then it is the reserve, in part. I propose 2,000 from reserve, 1,300 from postage and printing, which is fat we can render by going to email notices a year early. Marchetti: People like the postcards. Treasurer Holm: People like heat more. Chair Ambrose: Motion is Holm's split: 2,000 reserve, 1,300 postage and printing, series and shelving untouched. Moved, Kwon. Seconded, Marchetti, with regret about the postcards. All in favor. Carried, five to none. The postcards get a farewell notice in the newsletter.
question: How many members did the library gain after last spring's author series?

passage: Verbatim record, Dorne Harbor moorings committee, annual allocation meeting. Chair Beckett: Forty-one moorings, fifty-three applications, same arithmetic as every year. Waiting list first. Sadler: Top of the list is Gunnarsson, waited four years. Then the Pell sisters, three years. Then Ost, also three, but Ost's application lapsed in the spring and restarted, so the tie breaks to the Pells. Chair Beckett: Vacancies this year? Sadler: Three. Kerridge sold up, the Marlin was condemned after the survey, and old Fenwick has moved to the river. So Gunnarsson, the Pells, and, by the tiebreak, Ost misses again. Voice, from the floor, Mr. Ost: Fourth year running, and I will say it plainly: the lapse was the harbor office losing my form, not me. Chair Beckett: Noted, Mr. Ost, and the office concedes the form was found behind a radiator. Committee, the rule says a lapse is a lapse regardless of fault. Do we apply it or amend it? Trevayne: Amend. A man should not lose his place to a radiator. Sadler: Amending mid-allocation reorders the list retroactively. Where does that end? Chair Beckett: Proposal from the chair: rule stands this year, but the committee grants Ost a supernumerary berth at the fuel pontoon for the season, and first refusal on the next vacancy, with the office's apology entered in the minutes. Moved, seconded, carried six to one, Sadler against on principle. Mr. Ost: Accepted, and I want the radiator checked yearly. Laughter. Chair Beckett: The clerk will so minute.
question: Where was Mr. Ost's lost form found?

passage: Transcript, product meeting, Bramblewick Preserves, new season planning. Onslow, production: The damson crop is the story this year. Our growers are reporting sixty percent of normal after the frost, and what there is, is small. Reyes, sales: Small is fine for jam. Sixty percent is not. The damson line was 41,000 jars last year and our best margin. Onslow: We can run maybe 26,000 jars honestly. After that we are buying fruit from the wholesale market at prices that eat the margin, or stretching with apple, which I will not put my name to. Petit, the kitchen: Grandmother clause: our label says damson, it is damson. The day it is damson and apple, the label says so in the same size letters. That was the founder's rule and it is why the shops trust us. Reyes: Agreed, nobody is arguing. I am asking what we sell in the gap. Petit: Greengage. The crop is heavy this year, the growers are begging, and greengage jam sold out in three weeks the one year we made it, 2018. Onslow: Because we only made 4,000 jars. Reyes: Scarcity did not hurt the story. Run 20,000 greengage, cap damson at 26,000, and I will sell the shortage as what it is, a frost year, honestly labeled. The trade respects a straight answer. Onslow: Kitchen? Petit: The kitchen can do it if the fruit starts by the 20th. Reyes: Then it is decided, pending the owner's nod, which I will get by Friday.
question: How many damson jars can production honestly run this year?

passage: Minutes kept verbatim, Nethercombe parish council, item five, the church clock. Chair Dunmore: The clock has stopped at twenty to four since August, and the tourists photograph it, which is not the reputation we want. Estimates, please. Clerk: Two received. Harben and Son, the firm that has serviced it since 1971, quotes 6,400 dollars, which includes releading the weight channel. A new firm, ChronoServe, quotes 3,900, but on inspection by ladder only, and their surveyor spent forty minutes in the tower against Harben's half day. Prowse: I rang three parishes that used ChronoServe. Two content, one clock stopped again within the year, and the firm argued the warranty. Fenn: Harben is a widow and one son now. If we pass them over for a cheaper survey, we lose them, and then every parish within thirty miles has lost them. Chair Dunmore: That is sentiment, Mr. Fenn. Fenn: It is infrastructure, Madam Chair. The sentiment is the clock. Prowse: I move Harben at 6,400, the difference from the fabric fund, subject to the son himself doing the regulating, as his father would have. Fenn: Second. Chair Dunmore: Carried, six in favor, one against, Mrs. Ashworth, who wants it minuted that the fabric fund exists for the roof, and that when the roof leaks she will read this minute aloud. So minuted. The clock goes to Harben.
question: At what time has the church clock been stopped since August?

passage: Transcript, safety briefing, Alderfen wind farm, maintenance crew, Monday. Supervisor Grieve: Three items, then the van. One: turbine 9 is locked out. The gearbox oil sample came back with metal in it, so nobody climbs 9 until the borescope on Thursday. The lockout is mine, the key is in the cabinet, and the tag says my name, which means the only person who unlocks it is me, not whoever is nearest when the phone rings. Understood? Crew: Understood. Grieve: Two: the weather window. We have today and tomorrow below 12 meters per second, then Wednesday gusts to 25. All tower work compresses into today and tomorrow, which means the annual on turbine 4 and the blade inspection on 7 run in parallel, separate teams, separate radios, channel 2 and channel 5, and nobody monkeys between teams without telling both leads. Kowalski: Channel 5 crackles near the substation. Grieve: Then channel 6, thank you, and I will have the radio tech look at 5. Three: the osprey platform on the met mast has a nest with two chicks, confirmed Friday. The ecologist's buffer is 300 meters for vehicles during fledging, so the track past the mast is closed and we go round by the north gate, which adds nine minutes. The company that ignored one of these buffers last year is still paying for it, and their name is not going to be ours. Questions? None? Van in five.
question: Which turbine is locked out pending the borescope?

passage: Verbatim minutes, Pelham Street market traders association, emergency session on the parking change. Chair Okoye: The council's letter, everyone has read it. Loading bay hours cut to 7 to 9 in the morning, enforcement cameras from the first of next month. Reactions, briefly, then a plan. Vasquez, fish: Briefly? My deliveries land at 11, when the boats have sorted. The 7 to 9 window is written by someone who has never met a fish. Adler, flowers: The Dutch lorry reaches us Tuesdays at noon. It cannot circle the ring road until Wednesday. Chair Okoye: Petition or meeting first? Brandt, hardware: Neither. Data first. My son works in an office that measures things for a living, and his advice was: count first, argue with numbers. I propose every trader logs deliveries for two weeks, time, duration, vehicle, and we present the council a load pattern instead of a complaint. Vasquez: While the cameras fine us? Chair Okoye: The letter says enforcement from the first, which gives us nineteen days. Two weeks of logging still fits. Adler: And if the numbers show most deliveries do fit 7 to 9? Brandt: Then some of us adjust, and the rest of us argue the exceptions honestly. Numbers cut both ways, that is their virtue. Chair Okoye: Motion: two week delivery log, all traders, forms from Brandt by Thursday, findings to the council with a request to delay enforcement one month. Moved, Brandt. Seconded, Vasquez, grudgingly. Carried unanimously. Mrs. Adler will mind the petition urge until we see the count.
question: What are the new loading bay hours in the council's letter?

passage: Transcript, rehearsal committee, Foxlow Amateur Operatic Society, casting dispute session, chair's recording. Chair Pemberton: The committee has heard the audition panel's report. For the role of the countess, the panel splits: two for Mrs. Delacroix, two for Miss Ivens. The constitution sends split castings here. Views, and keep them kind, this is a village and we all buy bread from Mrs. Delacroix's husband. Ng: Vocally, Ivens, and it is not close. The score sits high and Mrs. Delacroix transposed her audition piece down a third, which the panel noted. Harwood: And theatrically, Delacroix. She has held the second act finale together for twenty years. Ivens is twenty-three and has never carried a show past the interval. Ng: She will never carry one if we never hand her one. Chair Pemberton: The panel's own scoring sheet: Ivens 34 of 40 for voice, 22 for stage craft. Delacroix 26 for voice, 35 for stage craft. Harwood: Then the sheet says what we all said, and settles nothing. Chair Pemberton: The chair proposes what the sheet suggests: Ivens sings the countess, Delacroix is named associate director for the production, credited on the poster, with the second act finale hers to stage. We stop pretending one role must hold two kinds of excellence. Ng: Will Delacroix accept it? Harwood: If the poster credit is real and the finale is truly hers, I believe she will, and I will make the call myself. Chair Pemberton: Moved, seconded, carried four to nil. The call is Mr. Harwood's tonight, before the bakery opens tomorrow.
question: What score did Miss Ivens receive for voice on the panel's sheet?

passage: Minutes, taken in full, Grendel Row allotments water subcommittee. Chair Ibarra: One item: the trough tap on the top path failed its pressure test, and the plumber found the feed pipe is lead. Everything below the middle path is modern plastic from the 2004 works, but the top six plots have been watering from a lead feed since, apparently, the coronation. Reactions. Szabo: Which coronation? Chair Ibarra: The plumber's joke, Mr. Szabo, the pipe is very old. The health advice in the plumber's letter: lead uptake in vegetables is real but small, highest in leafy crops, and the sensible course is replacement, not panic. Quote: 2,800 dollars to trench and lay plastic to the top trough. Mrs. Okafor: The subcommittee's whole balance is 1,900. Szabo: Levy the six top plots? Mrs. Okafor: The six include two pensioners and the Youngs, who have had the year they have had. I will not means test a water pipe. Chair Ibarra: Alternative from the plumber: he will supply pipe and fittings at cost, 900 dollars, if we dig the trench ourselves. It is 80 meters, spade depth, through ground we all dig for a hobby. Szabo: Now that is an allotment answer. Working party, two weekends, I will bring the line and the son-in-law. Mrs. Okafor: The society's insurance covers volunteer works, I checked after the pond incident. Chair Ibarra: Motion: pipe at cost, trench by working party, first digging Saturday the 14th, tea rota to be argued about separately and at greater length. Carried, three to nil, and the clerk notes the laughter.
question: How much will the plumber charge for pipe and fittings at cost?
